                             4. Conclusions

                           The conducted studies on the tribological properties of friction pairs composed of a
                    DMLSed 20MnCr5 countersample and different types of metal sheets allowed to determine
                            the changes in the character of the friction process depending on the type of these friction
                                pairs. Based on the experimental studies, the following conclusions can be drawn:

                         •   The most stable friction force variations during wear tests were recorded for friction
                                   pairs of the 20MnCr5 countersample with Inconel 625 and 321 steel sheets. These sheets
                            were characterised by the highest strength among all the analysed sheets. For these
                                    sheets, similar COFs were observed during the entire wear test (COF = 0.194−0.213).
                           The remaining sheets with increased plasticity showed significantly higher values of
                                 the coefficient of friction (COF = 1.234 for the 20MnCr5/EN AW-6061 T0 friction pair
                           and COF = 0.813 for the 20MnCr5/pure copper friction pair).
                         •   The largest gain of countersample mass was observed for the 20MnCr5/EN AW-
                              6061 T0 friction pair. The sample mass loss in this combination was also the largest,
                             amounting to 19.96% of the initial mass. A similar behaviour of friction pair materials
                          was observed for the 20MnCr5/pure copper friction configuration. On the other hand,
                                     for the 20MnCr5/Inconel 625 friction pair, no significant changes in the mass of friction
                                  pair materials were observed.
                         •   During the friction of pure copper and the EN AW-6061 T0 sheet, the main friction
                            mechanism resulting from the high plasticity of these materials was adhesive wear. In
                                    contrast, in the 20MnCr5/Inconel 625 and 20MnCr5/321 steel friction pairs, abrasive
                            wear dominated.
                         •   Based on the changes in friction force, COFs, and mass changes in friction pair compo-
                                nents during wear tests, it can be concluded that potential tools in the form of inserts
                                or working layers manufactured using 3D printing technology, the DMLS method,
                              without additional surface treatment can be successfully used for stamping sheets of
                               321 steel and Inconel 625. These sheets are characterised by a low mass loss, the lowest
                            COFs, and stability of the friction force during the wear test.

                                Three-dimensional printing-aided rapid tooling is expected to have a major industrial
                          impact on the design and production of stamping tools. The implementation of 3D metal
                            printing can enhance the technology in flexible manufacturing systems according to the
                           concept of Industry 5.0. Although the number of metal grades for use in DMLS is still lim-
                                  ited, intensive work is underway on the development of new powders and the adaptation
                              of existing technologies along with the expansion of the part design space.

## pqac-00000014

From text 'zaba2024applicationofpowderbed pages 3-6'.

Krzysztof Żaba, Maciej Balcerzak, Łukasz Kuczek, Marcel Wiewióra, Ilona Różycka, Tomasz Trzepieciński, and Jarosław Mizera. Application of powder-bed fusion of metals using a laser for manufacturing of m300 maraging steel tools intended for sheet metal bending. Materials, 17:6185, Dec 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17246185, doi:10.3390/ma17246185. This article has 9 citations.

The Żaba 2024 M300 study reports detailed PBF-LB/M process parameters for manufacturing maraging steel M300 tools using an Xact Metal XM200C printer. Key parameters include: laser spot size 100 µm, laser speed 250-550 mm/s (contour to fill), laser power 50-80 W (contour to fill), layer thickness 0.03 mm, fill border offset 0.1 mm, offset transition area 0.1 mm, area tolerance 0.25 mm, number of exposures 2, and sorting method against gas flow. The M300 powder had a particle size distribution of 20-90 µm. These parameters were based on manufacturer guidelines. However, the excerpt does not report hatch spacing or hatch rotation values. The document also does not contain information about the Żaba 2025 20MnCr5 or Elhadad 2025 316L studies referenced in the question.

                                   4. Summary and Conclusions

                               This paper presents the results of research on bending tools made of maraging steel
                          manufactured using the PBF-LB/M technique. The design section of the paper was devoted
                             to the fabrication of tools using 3D printing technology. The condition of the tool was
                          analysed immediately after the 3D printing process was completed. The focus was on
                          a detailed assessment of the tool after its use in simulated industrial conditions in order
                              to determine its efficiency and durability in real operating conditions. Finally, tests were
                         conducted on the drawpieces obtained using the additively manufactured tool. This
                          enabled the asassessment of the efficiency and quality of the formed sheet metal elements
                       and tool wear after 3D printing.
                             Based on the research results, the following conclusions were formulated.

                                   1.   As a result of the sheet metal forming process, the hardness of the punch material
                                 increased in relation to the punch before forming. This increase was at a level equal
                                        to, on average, 6%. The hardness of the printed punches made of maraging steel
                         M300 using the PBF-LB/M method is approximately 360 HV1. The highest hardness
                                value was measured for the punch used to form the Inconel 625 sheet (357 HV1). The
                                  highest standard deviation value of 62.80 HV1 was measured for the Inconel 625 alloy
                              drawpiece formed using polished punch.
                                   2.   The outer surface of the tested steel is uneven, which is related to the printing process.
                                   3.   Microscopic observations of sheets after pressing using tools after 3D printing without
                                  additional processing and after polishing do not show significant differences.
                                   4.   M300 maraging steel is characterized by minimum of porosity after the printing
                                  process. An analysis of the chemical composition using the EDS method confirmed
                                 the presence of oxygen in these areas.
                                   5.    Tribological tests showed that in the case of the friction pair M300 steel and AW-6061
                           T0 aluminium alloy, an increase in the countersample mass by 0.06% was observed.
                         Due to the tendency of aluminium alloys to galling, part of the worn aluminium alloy
                          was deposited on the working surface of the countersample made of M300 steel.
                                   6.   The lowest coefficient of friction (µ = 0.518) was observed in the case of friction
                                  pair Inconel 625 and M300 steel, which explains the high share of oxides on the
                               countersample surface and the dominant abrasive wear mechanism.
                                   7.   Geometric measurements showed that both types of tools (without finishing and after
                                    polishing), showed wear resulting from high forming force. The tools were deformed

                                   in the part of the tool used as a substrate for 3D printing. The printed layers were
                            deformed due to the low strength of the base material (S235 structural steel).

                                 In plastic forming processes, one of the basic problems is the durability of tools,
                          which, in addition to high dimensional and shape accuracy, should ensure obtaining the
                           appropriate quality of products for the longest possible time of their operation. In the
                          heterogeneous tool–sheet–lubricant system, there are phenomena of adhesive wear of the
                             contact surface of the tools and the formed sheet, friction wear caused by the presence of
                             impurities on the surface of the sheet and wear products, and fatigue wear resulting from
                               cyclic and time-varying pressures and temperatures. Due to the complexity of the tool
                             destruction mechanism, a quantitative description of these processes is very difficult and
                             of little use for the needs of engineering design of plastic forming processes. A practical
                       method of reducing excessive tool wear is the use of highly resistant protective coatings on
                              tools and the introduction of tools made of non-metallic materials, including elastomeric
                       and composite materials.  In each of the above cases, an important role is played by
                            technological lubricants resistant to strength and temperature, dedicated to individual
                           process conditions. Currently used technological processes of sheet metal forming to
                         produce parts for, among others, the aviation and automotive industries are implemented
                           using conventional tool steels as tool material.
                        Due to the very wide range of production, relatively low service life of tools, and
                           high costs of their production and regeneration, work has been undertaken to develop and
                         implement innovative solutions using 3D metal printing to produce working parts of tools
                               for the plastic forming of sheets made of alloys such as Al and Ni.
                         As part of the research, sheet forming tools were produced, consisting of a base part
                             (base) made by machining from relatively cheap S235 steel, on which a working layer of

                                     is impossible when producing tools using the classic machining method. The main goal of
                             the research was to determine the usability of such tools without additional heat treatment,
                        which would contribute to the increase in the cost of tool production.
                                Furthermore, 3D printing technology allows for the free design of product morphology,
                           ensuring control over product properties. An extremely important advantage of the tech-
                          nology used is the ability to control the morphology and texture of the layer from the level
                              of a computer program used to design the 3D printing process. Obtaining the appropriate
                             surface morphology will increase the oil volume in the metal–tool contact surface and, as
                          a result, improve the tribological operating conditions during plastic forming using tools
                         with layers applied using 3D printing. The high level of process control, including the
                        volume of individual layers, sintering power, etc., is highly competitive with conventional
                        methods of producing coatings for stamping tools. Layers made using the 3D metal print-
                            ing method are characterized by a multi-layer structure and appropriate porosity obtained

                              lubricant in the deformation zone, reducing the coefficient of friction between the surface of
                             the coating and the surface of the shaped material, and thus, reducing tool wear. Currently,

{"answer": "# Peer-reviewed uses of Xact Metal LPBF printers

## Search result and scope

I found **three publications whose accessible full text explicitly says that specimens or parts were fabricated on an Xact Metal machine**: two journal articles using the **XM200C** and one IEEE conference paper using the **XM200G**. I did not find a full-text-verifiable academic example for the **XM200S or XM300 series**, nor a thesis or paper explicitly centered on using an Xact Metal printer in university teaching. “Not reported” below means that the publication did not provide the requested parameter, not that the machine lacked control of it.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

## Detailed evidence

### 1. M300 maraging-steel bending tools—XM200C

**Citation:** K. Żaba, M. Balcerzak, Ł. Kuczek, M. Wiewióra, I. Różycka, T. Trzepieciński, and J. Mizera, “Application of Powder-Bed Fusion of Metals Using a Laser for Manufacturing of M300 Maraging Steel Tools Intended for Sheet Metal Bending,” *Materials*, vol. 17, article 6185, 2024. DOI: **10.3390/ma17246185**. The paper identifies an Xact Metal **XM200C** and describes printing M300/1.2709 maraging-steel working portions directly on S235 structural-steel punch substrates. The resulting punches were tested by bending Inconel 625 and AW-6061 T0 sheet; those sheet alloys were workpieces, not LPBF feedstocks. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005)

**Reported parameters:** 50 W for contours and 80 W for fill; 250 mm/s for contours and 550 mm/s for fill; 30 µm layers; 100 µm laser spot; two exposures; 0.1 mm fill-border offset; 0.1 mm transition-area offset; 0.25 mm area tolerance; and sorting against gas flow. Hatch spacing and interlayer hatch-rotation angle were not reported. The authors state that these settings were based on the printer manufacturer’s guidance for M300 powder, rather than presenting them as a newly optimized open parameter set. (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000014)

**Capability demonstrated:** The XM200C produced functional, near-minimally porous M300 working layers. The un-heat-treated, as-printed tools were usable for bending within a defined force range. Relative to the company’s conventional process, the authors reported a reduction from 80 to 48 hours, from 18 to 7 operations, and from about EUR 3,500 to EUR 1,500. They also emphasized the ability to vary working-part geometry and to control layer morphology through the process software. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016)

**Limitations demonstrated:** The outer surface was uneven because of the printing process, local pores produced hardness reductions, and both as-printed and polished tools deformed under high forming force. The authors attributed especially important deformation to the lower strength of the S235 substrate rather than solely to the printed M300. They concluded that LPBF tooling remained less strong and durable than conventional heat-treated tooling and required further optimization, potentially including heat treatment, surface treatment, laser remelting/alloying, or coatings. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016)

### 2. 20MnCr5 tribological countersamples—XM200C

**Citation:** K. Żaba, M. Madej, B. Leszczyńska-Madej, T. Trzepieciński, and R. Sitek, “Tribological Performance of Direct Metal Laser Sintered 20MnCr5 Tool Steel Countersamples Designed for Sheet Metal Forming Applications,” *Applied Sciences*, vol. 15, article 8711, 2025. DOI: **10.3390/app15158711**. The authors printed 20MnCr5/1.7147 tool-steel countersamples on an Xact Metal **XM200C**, then tested them against Inconel 625, type 321 stainless steel, AW-6061 T0 aluminum, and pure-copper sheet specimens. Only 20MnCr5 was printed; the other materials were tribological counterpart sheets. (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000012)

**Reported parameters:** 110 W laser power, 600 mm/s scan speed, 20 µm layers, 100 µm beam diameter, and a meander strategy rotating the scanning angle by 67° between successive layers. The paper reports a 100 µm “scanning distance.” This appears to serve the role normally described as hatch/scan-line spacing, but the authors’ terminology should be retained rather than treating that interpretation as certain. (pqac-00000012)

**Capability demonstrated:** Without additional surface treatment, XM200C-produced 20MnCr5 was judged potentially suitable for stamping-tool inserts or working layers used against 321 stainless steel and Inconel 625. These pairs had stable friction, coefficients of friction of approximately 0.194–0.213, and little mass loss; the Inconel pair showed no significant mass change. The work therefore demonstrates processing of a less-standard tool steel with a fully disclosed custom parameter combination and scan strategy. (pqac-00000013)

**Limitations demonstrated:** Performance was strongly counter-material-dependent. AW-6061 T0 and copper underwent pronounced adhesive wear and material transfer onto the printed countersample; the aluminum pair had a COF of 1.234 and 19.96% sheet mass loss. The authors also identified the still-limited number of metal grades available for DMLS as a broader limitation, although they noted continuing powder/process development. (pqac-00000013)

### 3. Porous 316L microbial-fuel-cell electrodes—XM200G

**Citation:** A. Elhadad, G. Li, J. Yang, D. Liu, and S. Choi, “3D-Printed Stainless Steel Electrodes for Advancing MEMS Microbial Fuel Cells Toward Sustainable On-Chip Energy,” in *2025 IEEE 38th International Conference on Micro Electro Mechanical Systems (MEMS)*, pp. 643–646, 2025. DOI: **10.1109/MEMS61431.2025.10918293**. The authors used 316L powder and an Xact Metal **XM200G**, equipped with a nominal 200 W laser, to fabricate porous stainless-steel anode/electrode structures. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003)

**Reported parameters:** 180 W laser power, 400 mm/s scan speed, 100 µm hatch spacing, 30 µm layers, and an argon atmosphere. Hatch-rotation angle was not reported. The authors say that the key parameters were “optimized to achieve high-quality prints,” so this is evidence that users could apply a study-specific parameter set; however, the short paper does not describe the optimization design, parameter bounds, firmware access, or whether every machine control was open. (pqac-00000003)

**Capability demonstrated:** The XM200G fabricated diverse 3D microporous sizes and shapes with porosity suitable for bacterial attachment and electron transfer. The resulting electrodes supported easy catalyst modification, retained bioelectrochemical activity without evident degradation, and were stable and reusable over multiple cycles. The assembled microbial fuel cell reached 127 µW maximum power and 750 µA peak current, outperforming the alternative miniature-MFC substrates used for comparison. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000001)

**Limitations evident from the publication:** The conference paper does not provide hatch rotation, contour parameters, porosity-design parameters, density, processing-window limits, or optimization methodology. Thus, it establishes successful customized 316L processing and geometric control but cannot support conclusions about the XM200G’s entire parameter envelope or repeatability across machines. (pqac-00000003)

## Teaching, education, and open/custom parameters

* **Teaching/education:** No retrieved peer-reviewed article, conference paper, or thesis explicitly described an Xact Metal machine being used as part of a university course, laboratory class, student-training program, or pedagogical intervention. All three verified studies involved university researchers, but that is not equivalent to evidence of teaching use.
* **Open/custom processing:** The 2024 M300 study exposes numerous editable build settings in Materialise Magics but says that the chosen values followed Xact Metal manufacturer guidance. The 20MnCr5 study reports a distinct material-specific parameter combination and 67° rotating meander strategy, although it does not explicitly call the machine “open.” The 316L study explicitly says its parameters were optimized, but provides neither the optimization protocol nor a claim of open firmware/control. Accordingly, these papers support **user-set or study-specific parameters**, but not the stronger assertion that Xact Metal offers a fully open-control LPBF platform. (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000003)

## Overall assessment

The verified literature is small but shows two principal capabilities: the XM200C can process M300 and 20MnCr5 tool steels into functional tooling or tribological specimens, while the XM200G can produce tailored porous 316L electrochemical structures. The strongest recurring limitations are incomplete reporting of hatch variables, as-built roughness and occasional porosity, dependence on substrate and mating material, and lack of a documented broad processing window. No verified publication in the retrieved corpus establishes use of an XM200S/XM300, formal educational deployment, or fully open machine control."}

# Summary

This peer-reviewed article examines tribological performance of 20MnCr5 tool steel countersamples produced by Direct Metal Laser Sintering (DMLS) for sheet metal forming applications. The study tested DMLS-produced countersamples against various materials including "Inconel 625, titanium-stabilised stainless steel 321, EN AW-6061 T0 aluminium alloy, and pure copper" under dry friction conditions using a roller-block tribotester.

Key findings include: the 20MnCr5/EN AW-6061 T0 friction pair showed largest mass loss (19.96%), while the 20MnCr5/Inconel 625 pair showed minimal changes (0.04% loss). Coefficient of friction values ranged from 0.194-0.213 (stable) to 1.234 (highest). The study concluded that "tools in the form of inserts or working layers manufactured using 3D printing technology, the DMLS method, without additional surface treatment can be successfully used for forming sheets of 321 steel and Inconel 625."

**Note:** The excerpt does not specify an Xact Metal machine model or detailed process parameters (laser power, scan speed, hatch spacing, layer thickness, hatch rotation angle).

This excerpt discusses tribological properties of friction pairs using a DMLS (Direct Metal Laser Sintering) 3D-printed 20MnCr5 countersample tested against various metal sheets including Inconel 625, 321 steel, pure copper, and EN AW-6061 T0 aluminum alloy. The paper mentions DMLS as a rapid tooling technology with potential industrial impact, noting that "the number of metal grades for use in DMLS is still limited." snippets: The following 3D printing parameters were set: sorting method—against gas flow, fill border offset—0.1 mm, number of exposures—2, offset transition area—0.1 mm, area tolerance—0.25 mm, and fill border offset—0.1 mm. The laser spot size was 100 microns, and the offset was set to 0.1 mm. The laser speed ranged from 250 mm·s−1 for the contour to 550 mm·s−1 for the fill. The laser power was regulated from 50 W for the contour to 80 W for the fill. The layer thickness was 0.03 mm.

For 3D printing using the PBF-LB/M method, gas-atomized M300 maraging steel powder (Figure 2) was used, supplied by Electro Optical Systems GmbH (Krailling, Germany), together with a quality control certificate, characterized by a particle size distribution in the range of 20 to 90 µm.
The bases for these settings were the guidelines proposed by the manufacturer of the 3D printer for printing powder from maraging M300 steel.

# Summary

This excerpt discusses using 3D metal printing (PBF-LB/M - powder bed fusion laser beam metal) to produce sheet forming tools with a machined steel base and a printed working layer made of M300 steel. The research aimed to determine tool usability "without additional heat treatment, which would contribute to the increase in the cost of tool production." 

Key advantages noted include: free design of product morphology, control over porosity and surface texture via "3D printing parameters (temperature, sintering speed, amount of powder fed to the sintering zone at one time, powder grain size)," and reduced friction coefficients for tool steel-aluminum pairs. Hardness testing showed "relatively even" distribution in the printed layer, with "local reduction in hardness values" due to pores. The study prioritized "reducing production time and costs while meeting the technical requirements for tool functionality" rather than matching conventional stamps' strength.

However, **this excerpt does not cite specific Xact Metal machine models, peer-reviewed citations, or detailed process parameters requested in the question.**

# Summary

This excerpt describes research on bending tools manufactured from maraging steel M300 using "PBF-LB/M technique" (powder bed fusion laser beam/metal additive manufacturing). However, **the excerpt does not specify an Xact Metal machine model** or mention Xact Metal by name. 

Key findings include: printed punches showed approximately 360 HV1 hardness with ~6% increase after forming; M300 steel exhibited "minimum of porosity after the printing process"; tools functioned without additional heat treatment; and production time was 48 hours versus 80 hours for conventional methods with 60% cost reduction. The study concludes that while PBF-LB/M tools "have the potential to revolutionize tool production," they "currently require further development and optimisation," with future work planned on heat treatment and surface coatings.

**Note:** This excerpt does not provide the specific information requested (Xact Metal model, detailed process parameters, or direct machine capability conclusions).

Question: Find examples of peer-reviewed academic literature (journal articles, conference papers, theses) in which an Xact Metal laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) metal 3D printer was used to fabricate or study parts. Xact Metal models include the XM200C, XM200G, XM200S, and XM300 series. For each example found, report: the citation, the Xact Metal model used, the material(s) printed (e.g., 316L, 17-4PH, AlSi10Mg, Inconel 718, bronze, copper), the process parameters reported (laser power, scan speed, hatch spacing, layer thickness, hatch rotation angle), and what the study concluded about the machine's capabilities or limitations. Also note any papers describing use of Xact Metal machines in university teaching/education or with open/custom process parameters.

# Peer-reviewed uses of Xact Metal LPBF printers

## Search result and scope

I found **three publications whose accessible full text explicitly says that specimens or parts were fabricated on an Xact Metal machine**: two journal articles using the **XM200C** and one IEEE conference paper using the **XM200G**. I did not find a full-text-verifiable academic example for the **XM200S or XM300 series**, nor a thesis or paper explicitly centered on using an Xact Metal printer in university teaching. “Not reported” below means that the publication did not provide the requested parameter, not that the machine lacked control of it.

| Short citation | Model | Printed material / part | Laser power | Scan speed | Hatch spacing | Layer thickness | Hatch rotation | Parameter openness / source | Demonstrated capability and limitations |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Żaba et al., *Materials* 2024, 17, 6185. DOI: 10.3390/ma17246185 | XM200C | M300 maraging steel working layer on S235 steel bending punches; used to form Inconel 625 and AW-6061 T0 sheets | 50 W contour to 80 W fill | 250 mm/s contour to 550 mm/s fill | not reported | 0.03 mm (30 µm) | not reported | Based on manufacturer guidelines for printing maraging M300 steel; additional settings reported: sorting method against gas flow, fill border offset 0.1 mm, number of exposures 2, offset transition area 0.1 mm, area tolerance 0.25 mm, laser spot 100 µm (zaba2024applicationofpowderbed pages 3-6) | Showed suitability of as-printed, un-heat-treated M300 tools for bending in a certain force range; any working-part shape could be produced, with reported tool-production time and cost reductions versus conventional tooling. Limitations: uneven outer surface from printing, local porosity, deformation due to weaker S235 substrate, and need for further optimization/treatments for greater durability (zaba2024applicationofpowderbed pages 23-25, zaba2024applicationofpowderbed pages 22-23) |
| Żaba et al., *Applied Sciences* 2025, 15, 8711. DOI: 10.3390/app15158711 | XM200C | 20MnCr5 steel DMLS countersamples for tribological study against Inconel 625, 321 stainless steel, EN AW-6061 T0 aluminum alloy, and pure copper sheets | 110 W | 600 mm/s | 100 µm scanning distance (paper’s term; likely hatch spacing) | 20 µm | 67° change in scanning angle between successive layers | Custom process details reported in the paper: meandering scan strategy, fibre-laser XM200C, beam diameter 100 µm (zaba2025tribologicalperformanceof pages 4-6) | Demonstrated that DMLS 20MnCr5 could serve as insert/working-layer material for stamping 321 steel and Inconel 625 without additional surface treatment, with low/stable COF and low mass loss. Limitations: severe adhesive wear/material transfer with AW-6061 T0 and Cu; authors also note the limited number of metal grades available for DMLS despite ongoing development (zaba2025tribologicalperformanceof pages 16-18) |
| Elhadad et al., IEEE MEMS 2025, pp. 643–646. DOI: 10.1109/MEMS61431.2025.10918293 | XM200G | 316L stainless steel porous anodes/electrodes for MEMS microbial fuel cells | 180 W | 400 mm/s | 100 µm | 30 µm | not reported | Paper states key printing parameters were optimized to achieve high-quality prints; 200 W laser machine, argon atmosphere (elhadad20253dprintedstainlesssteel pages 2-4) | Demonstrated the XM200G could fabricate tailored 3D microporous 316L structures with controllable porosity/shape, high stability, reusability, and strong MFC performance; enabled straightforward catalyst surface modification. Limitation: no hatch rotation or broader processing-window details reported in the conference paper (elhadad20253dprintedstainlesssteel pages 1-2, elhadad20253dprintedstainlesssteel pages 2-4) |


*Table: This table compares the three full-text-verified peer-reviewed publications found to explicitly use Xact Metal LPBF printers, including model, material, reported process parameters, and the capabilities or limitations each study demonstrated.*

## Detailed evidence

### 1. M300 maraging-steel bending tools—XM200C

**Citation:** K. Żaba, M. Balcerzak, Ł. Kuczek, M. Wiewióra, I. Różycka, T. Trzepieciński, and J. Mizera, “Application of Powder-Bed Fusion of Metals Using a Laser for Manufacturing of M300 Maraging Steel Tools Intended for Sheet Metal Bending,” *Materials*, vol. 17, article 6185, 2024. DOI: **10.3390/ma17246185**. The paper identifies an Xact Metal **XM200C** and describes printing M300/1.2709 maraging-steel working portions directly on S235 structural-steel punch substrates. The resulting punches were tested by bending Inconel 625 and AW-6061 T0 sheet; those sheet alloys were workpieces, not LPBF feedstocks. (zaba2024applicationofpowderbed pages 1-2, zaba2024applicationofpowderbed pages 3-6)

**Reported parameters:** 50 W for contours and 80 W for fill; 250 mm/s for contours and 550 mm/s for fill; 30 µm layers; 100 µm laser spot; two exposures; 0.1 mm fill-border offset; 0.1 mm transition-area offset; 0.25 mm area tolerance; and sorting against gas flow. Hatch spacing and interlayer hatch-rotation angle were not reported. The authors state that these settings were based on the printer manufacturer’s guidance for M300 powder, rather than presenting them as a newly optimized open parameter set. (zaba2024applicationofpowderbed pages 3-6)

**Capability demonstrated:** The XM200C produced functional, near-minimally porous M300 working layers. The un-heat-treated, as-printed tools were usable for bending within a defined force range. Relative to the company’s conventional process, the authors reported a reduction from 80 to 48 hours, from 18 to 7 operations, and from about EUR 3,500 to EUR 1,500. They also emphasized the ability to vary working-part geometry and to control layer morphology through the process software. (zaba2024applicationofpowderbed pages 23-25, zaba2024applicationofpowderbed pages 22-23)

**Limitations demonstrated:** The outer surface was uneven because of the printing process, local pores produced hardness reductions, and both as-printed and polished tools deformed under high forming force. The authors attributed especially important deformation to the lower strength of the S235 substrate rather than solely to the printed M300. They concluded that LPBF tooling remained less strong and durable than conventional heat-treated tooling and required further optimization, potentially including heat treatment, surface treatment, laser remelting/alloying, or coatings. (zaba2024applicationofpowderbed pages 23-25, zaba2024applicationofpowderbed pages 22-23)

### 2. 20MnCr5 tribological countersamples—XM200C

**Citation:** K. Żaba, M. Madej, B. Leszczyńska-Madej, T. Trzepieciński, and R. Sitek, “Tribological Performance of Direct Metal Laser Sintered 20MnCr5 Tool Steel Countersamples Designed for Sheet Metal Forming Applications,” *Applied Sciences*, vol. 15, article 8711, 2025. DOI: **10.3390/app15158711**. The authors printed 20MnCr5/1.7147 tool-steel countersamples on an Xact Metal **XM200C**, then tested them against Inconel 625, type 321 stainless steel, AW-6061 T0 aluminum, and pure-copper sheet specimens. Only 20MnCr5 was printed; the other materials were tribological counterpart sheets. (zaba2025tribologicalperformanceof pages 1-2, zaba2025tribologicalperformanceof pages 2-4, zaba2025tribologicalperformanceof pages 4-6)

**Reported parameters:** 110 W laser power, 600 mm/s scan speed, 20 µm layers, 100 µm beam diameter, and a meander strategy rotating the scanning angle by 67° between successive layers. The paper reports a 100 µm “scanning distance.” This appears to serve the role normally described as hatch/scan-line spacing, but the authors’ terminology should be retained rather than treating that interpretation as certain. (zaba2025tribologicalperformanceof pages 4-6)

**Capability demonstrated:** Without additional surface treatment, XM200C-produced 20MnCr5 was judged potentially suitable for stamping-tool inserts or working layers used against 321 stainless steel and Inconel 625. These pairs had stable friction, coefficients of friction of approximately 0.194–0.213, and little mass loss; the Inconel pair showed no significant mass change. The work therefore demonstrates processing of a less-standard tool steel with a fully disclosed custom parameter combination and scan strategy. (zaba2025tribologicalperformanceof pages 16-18)

**Limitations demonstrated:** Performance was strongly counter-material-dependent. AW-6061 T0 and copper underwent pronounced adhesive wear and material transfer onto the printed countersample; the aluminum pair had a COF of 1.234 and 19.96% sheet mass loss. The authors also identified the still-limited number of metal grades available for DMLS as a broader limitation, although they noted continuing powder/process development. (zaba2025tribologicalperformanceof pages 16-18)

### 3. Porous 316L microbial-fuel-cell electrodes—XM200G

**Citation:** A. Elhadad, G. Li, J. Yang, D. Liu, and S. Choi, “3D-Printed Stainless Steel Electrodes for Advancing MEMS Microbial Fuel Cells Toward Sustainable On-Chip Energy,” in *2025 IEEE 38th International Conference on Micro Electro Mechanical Systems (MEMS)*, pp. 643–646, 2025. DOI: **10.1109/MEMS61431.2025.10918293**. The authors used 316L powder and an Xact Metal **XM200G**, equipped with a nominal 200 W laser, to fabricate porous stainless-steel anode/electrode structures. (elhadad20253dprintedstainlesssteel pages 1-2, elhadad20253dprintedstainlesssteel pages 2-4)

**Reported parameters:** 180 W laser power, 400 mm/s scan speed, 100 µm hatch spacing, 30 µm layers, and an argon atmosphere. Hatch-rotation angle was not reported. The authors say that the key parameters were “optimized to achieve high-quality prints,” so this is evidence that users could apply a study-specific parameter set; however, the short paper does not describe the optimization design, parameter bounds, firmware access, or whether every machine control was open. (elhadad20253dprintedstainlesssteel pages 2-4)

**Capability demonstrated:** The XM200G fabricated diverse 3D microporous sizes and shapes with porosity suitable for bacterial attachment and electron transfer. The resulting electrodes supported easy catalyst modification, retained bioelectrochemical activity without evident degradation, and were stable and reusable over multiple cycles. The assembled microbial fuel cell reached 127 µW maximum power and 750 µA peak current, outperforming the alternative miniature-MFC substrates used for comparison. (elhadad20253dprintedstainlesssteel pages 2-4, elhadad20253dprintedstainlesssteel pages 4-4)

**Limitations evident from the publication:** The conference paper does not provide hatch rotation, contour parameters, porosity-design parameters, density, processing-window limits, or optimization methodology. Thus, it establishes successful customized 316L processing and geometric control but cannot support conclusions about the XM200G’s entire parameter envelope or repeatability across machines. (elhadad20253dprintedstainlesssteel pages 2-4)

## Teaching, education, and open/custom parameters

* **Teaching/education:** No retrieved peer-reviewed article, conference paper, or thesis explicitly described an Xact Metal machine being used as part of a university course, laboratory class, student-training program, or pedagogical intervention. All three verified studies involved university researchers, but that is not equivalent to evidence of teaching use.
* **Open/custom processing:** The 2024 M300 study exposes numerous editable build settings in Materialise Magics but says that the chosen values followed Xact Metal manufacturer guidance. The 20MnCr5 study reports a distinct material-specific parameter combination and 67° rotating meander strategy, although it does not explicitly call the machine “open.” The 316L study explicitly says its parameters were optimized, but provides neither the optimization protocol nor a claim of open firmware/control. Accordingly, these papers support **user-set or study-specific parameters**, but not the stronger assertion that Xact Metal offers a fully open-control LPBF platform. (zaba2024applicationofpowderbed pages 3-6, zaba2025tribologicalperformanceof pages 4-6, elhadad20253dprintedstainlesssteel pages 2-4)

## Overall assessment

The verified literature is small but shows two principal capabilities: the XM200C can process M300 and 20MnCr5 tool steels into functional tooling or tribological specimens, while the XM200G can produce tailored porous 316L electrochemical structures. The strongest recurring limitations are incomplete reporting of hatch variables, as-built roughness and occasional porosity, dependence on substrate and mating material, and lack of a documented broad processing window. No verified publication in the retrieved corpus establishes use of an XM200S/XM300, formal educational deployment, or fully open machine control.

info.query: Find examples of peer-reviewed academic literature (journal articles, conference papers, theses) in which an Xact Metal laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) metal 3D printer was used to fabricate or study parts. Xact Metal models include the XM200C, XM200G, XM200S, and XM300 series. For each example found, report: the citation, the Xact Metal model used, the material(s) printed (e.g., 316L, 17-4PH, AlSi10Mg, Inconel 718, bronze, copper), the process parameters reported (laser power, scan speed, hatch spacing, layer thickness, hatch rotation angle), and what the study concluded about the machine's capabilities or limitations. Also note any papers describing use of Xact Metal machines in university teaching/education or with open/custom process parameters.
